steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an article on the Algorithm Configuration Problem. Give some background, define the problem formally with its inputs, relate it to algorithm selection, say why it is hard and where it is used, and state what the article contributes.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Context: automatic configuration of algorithmic parameters; what the ACP is
2. Formal setup: target algorithm and the inputs of the ACP
3. Formal definition of the ACP
4. ASP as a special case; hardness; applications
5. What this article provides; abbreviations

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Context
- automatic configuration of algorithmic parameters: active research area; goes back to foundational work published in 1976
- ACP: parametrized algorithms deployed on instances of a decision/optimization problem; identify parameters giving best performance on the input

2. Formal setup
- \mathcal{A}: configurable target algorithm; input = problem instance + array of parameters ("algorithmic configuration")
- inputs of the ACP:
  - \Pi: problem solved by \mathcal{A}, (potentially) infinite set of instances; instance = string in an alphabet, usually ASCII/binary file encoding (vectors of) discrete/continuous values; \Pi endowed with a metric, \mathsf{dist}(\cdot,\cdot)\in\mathbb{R}, approaches zero for similar instances; \mathsf{dist} not necessarily unique, always closed algebraic form
  - \mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{A}}: parameter configurations, vectors of q continuous and/or discrete/categorical values (boolean, numeric, categorical); not all values admissible (domain constraints, logical conditions on multiple parameters) -> assume only feasible configurations
  - p_{\mathcal{A}}: performance function, (\pi,c) -> outcome of running \mathcal{A} configured by c on \pi; single continuous/discrete value; cost measure (CPU time, number of iterations) or quality measure (accuracy of ML predictor at some training iteration, integrality gap of optimization solver within time limit); minimize or maximize

3. Definition
- given (\mathcal{A},\pi,p_{\mathcal{A}}), \pi\in\Pi, find c^{\ast}_{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{A}} with optimal p_{\mathcal{A}} for solving \pi with \mathcal{A}

4. ASP, hardness, applications
- Algorithm Selection Problem (ASP): pick best of a set of configured algorithms for a specific instance
- choice of algorithm = one single parameter of a meta-algorithm for \Pi -> ASP special case of ACP
- very hard in theory and practice: many configurable parameters; closed-form expression of p_{\mathcal{A}} almost never available
- applications: configuring constraint programming / mathematical optimization solvers; hyperparameter tuning of ML pipelines; administration of ad-hoc medical treatments; many others
- pointer to more detailed treatments of the subject

5. This article
- comprehensive framework for describing any approach to the ACP
- core building components for an ACP solution strategy; use patterns and implementation
- Tab. 1: abbreviations

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
There is a lot of active research on configuring the parameters of algorithms automatically, and it goes back to foundational work that was published in 1976. The Algorithm Configuration Problem (ACP) is about parametrized algorithms that are used to solve instances of some decision or optimization problem. The question is which algorithmic parameters give the best performance when the algorithm is run on its input.

To be formal, let \mathcal{A} be a configurable target algorithm. The input of \mathcal{A} is an instance of the problem it solves and also an array of parameters, and we call this array the "algorithmic configuration".

The ACP has the following inputs:

- • \Pi: this is the decision/optimization problem that \mathcal{A} solves. It is a (potentially) infinite set of instances. An instance is usually described by a string in some alphabet, most of the time an ASCII or binary file that encodes the (vectors of) discrete/continuous values of the instance data. We assume that \Pi has a metric and that there is a function \mathsf{dist}(\cdot,\cdot)\in\mathbb{R} that measures the distance between points in \Pi and that approaches zero when two instances are similar. \mathsf{dist} does not have to be unique, but we assume that it is always given by an expression in closed algebraic form;

- • \mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{A}}: this is the set of parameter configurations of \mathcal{A}. Each configuration is usually encoded by a vector of q continuous and/or discrete/categorical values, and these represent parameters of different types (boolean, numeric, categorical). Some parameter values may not be admissible, because there are constraints on the domain of a parameter or logical conditions that involve several parameters. To keep it simple we assume that \mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{A}} contains only feasible algorithmic configurations;

- • p_{\mathcal{A}}: this is the performance function of \mathcal{A}. It maps a pair (\pi,c) (instance, parameter configuration) to the outcome of running \mathcal{A} with configuration c to solve the instance \pi. p_{\mathcal{A}} is encoded as a single continuous or discrete value. It can be a cost measure (e.g., CPU time, number of iterations performed, etc.) or it can be a quality measure (e.g., the accuracy of a Machine Learning (ML) predictor at a certain iteration of the training, the integrality gap that an optimization solver reports within a certain time limit, etc.). Depending on the case, we want to minimize it or maximize it.

3. Definition
- given (\mathcal{A},\pi,p_{\mathcal{A}}), \pi\in\Pi, find c^{\ast}_{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{A}} with optimal p_{\mathcal{A}} for solving \pi with \mathcal{A}

4. ASP, hardness, applications
- Algorithm Selection Problem (ASP): pick best of a set of configured algorithms for a specific instance
- choice of algorithm = one single parameter of a meta-algorithm for \Pi -> ASP special case of ACP
- very hard in theory and practice: many configurable parameters; closed-form expression of p_{\mathcal{A}} almost never available
- applications: configuring constraint programming / mathematical optimization solvers; hyperparameter tuning of ML pipelines; administration of ad-hoc medical treatments; many others
- pointer to more detailed treatments of the subject

5. This article
- comprehensive framework for describing any approach to the ACP
- core building components for an ACP solution strategy; use patterns and implementation
- Tab. 1: abbreviations

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
There is a lot of active research on configuring the parameters of algorithms automatically, and it goes back to foundational work that was published in 1976. The Algorithm Configuration Problem (ACP) is about parametrized algorithms that are used to solve instances of some decision or optimization problem. The question is which algorithmic parameters give the best performance when the algorithm is run on its input.

To be formal, let \mathcal{A} be a configurable target algorithm. The input of \mathcal{A} is an instance of the problem it solves and also an array of parameters, and we call this array the "algorithmic configuration".

The ACP has the following inputs:

- • \Pi: this is the decision/optimization problem that \mathcal{A} solves. It is a (potentially) infinite set of instances. An instance is usually described by a string in some alphabet, most of the time an ASCII or binary file that encodes the (vectors of) discrete/continuous values of the instance data. We assume that \Pi has a metric and that there is a function \mathsf{dist}(\cdot,\cdot)\in\mathbb{R} that measures the distance between points in \Pi and that approaches zero when two instances are similar. \mathsf{dist} does not have to be unique, but we assume that it is always given by an expression in closed algebraic form;

- • \mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{A}}: this is the set of parameter configurations of \mathcal{A}. Each configuration is usually encoded by a vector of q continuous and/or discrete/categorical values, and these represent parameters of different types (boolean, numeric, categorical). Some parameter values may not be admissible, because there are constraints on the domain of a parameter or logical conditions that involve several parameters. To keep it simple we assume that \mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{A}} contains only feasible algorithmic configurations;

- • p_{\mathcal{A}}: this is the performance function of \mathcal{A}. It maps a pair (\pi,c) (instance, parameter configuration) to the outcome of running \mathcal{A} with configuration c to solve the instance \pi. p_{\mathcal{A}} is encoded as a single continuous or discrete value. It can be a cost measure (e.g., CPU time, number of iterations performed, etc.) or it can be a quality measure (e.g., the accuracy of a Machine Learning (ML) predictor at a certain iteration of the training, the integrality gap that an optimization solver reports within a certain time limit, etc.). Depending on the case, we want to minimize it or maximize it.

With these specifications the ACP is defined formally like this:

Given a tuple (\mathcal{A},\pi,p_{\mathcal{A}}), \pi\in\Pi, find the algorithmic configuration c^{\ast}_{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{A}} providing the optimal performance p_{\mathcal{A}} for solving \pi with \mathcal{A}.

The Algorithm Selection Problem (ASP) is a variant of the ACP. In the ASP we want to pick the best algorithm for solving a specific instance from a given set of configured algorithms. But the choice of which algorithm to pick can be seen as the one single parameter of a meta-algorithm that solves \Pi, so the ASP is really a special case of the ACP. The ACP is very hard in general, both in theory and in practice. Algorithms may have a large number of parameters that can be configured, and a closed-form algebraic expression of p_{\mathcal{A}} is almost never available. Still, the ACP has a large number of very relevant applications, for example configuring constraint programming or mathematical optimization solvers (see, e.g., the work on solver tuning), tuning the hyperparameters of ML pipelines, administering ad-hoc medical treatments, and many others. For a more detailed treatment of the subject the interested reader can look at existing surveys and the references there.

In this article we give a comprehensive framework that can describe any approach to the ACP. We identify the core building components for designing a solution strategy for the ACP, and we discuss how they can be used and implemented.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Automatic configuration of algorithmic parameters is an area of active research [1,2], going back to the foundational work [3], published in 1976. The Algorithm Configuration Problem (ACP) concerns parametrized algorithms deployed to solve instances of a given decision or optimization problem. It is about identifying the algorithmic parameters that yield the best performance when the algorithm is run on its input.

Formally, let \mathcal{A} be a configurable target algorithm. Its input consists of an instance of the problem being solved and an array of parameters; we call the latter "algorithmic configuration".

The inputs of the ACP are:

- • \Pi: the decision/optimization problem to be solved by \mathcal{A}, consisting of a (potentially) infinite set of instances. Each instance is typically described by a string in an appropriate alphabet, most often an ASCII or binary file encoding the (vectors of) discrete/continuous values that characterize the instance data. We assume that \Pi is endowed with a metric and that there exists a function \mathsf{dist}(\cdot,\cdot)\in\mathbb{R} which measures the distance between points in \Pi and approaches zero if two instances are similar. The function \mathsf{dist} is not necessarily unique, but we assume that it is always defined by an expression in closed algebraic form;

- • \mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{A}}: the set of parameter configurations of \mathcal{A}, each usually encoded by a vector of q continuous and/or discrete/categorical values representing parameters of different types (boolean, numeric, categorical). Not all possible parameter values may be admissible, due to constraints on a parameter domain or logical conditions involving multiple parameters. For simplicity, we therefore assume that \mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{A}} only contains feasible algorithmic configurations;

- • p_{\mathcal{A}}: the performance function of \mathcal{A}, mapping a pair (\pi,c) (instance, parameter configuration) to the outcome of running \mathcal{A}, configured by c, to solve the instance \pi. p_{\mathcal{A}} is encoded as a single continuous or discrete value. The performance p_{\mathcal{A}} is either a cost measure (e.g., CPU time, number of iterations performed, etc.) or a quality measure (e.g., the accuracy achieved by a Machine Learning (ML) predictor at a certain iteration of the training process, the integrality gap reported by an optimization solver within a certain time limit, etc.). Depending on the case, one aims at minimizing or maximizing it.

With these specifications, the ACP is formally defined as follows:

Given a tuple (\mathcal{A},\pi,p_{\mathcal{A}}), \pi\in\Pi, find the algorithmic configuration c^{\ast}_{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{A}} providing the optimal performance p_{\mathcal{A}} for solving \pi with \mathcal{A}.

A variant of the ACP is the Algorithm Selection Problem (ASP), where one seeks to pick, from a given set of configured algorithms, the best one for solving a specific instance. However, the choice of which algorithm to pick can be seen as the one single parameter of a meta-algorithm for solving \Pi, so the ASP is a special case of the ACP. The ACP is generally very hard both in theory and in practice, since algorithms may have a large number of configurable parameters and a closed-form algebraic expression of p_{\mathcal{A}} is almost never available. Yet the ACP has many very relevant applications, such as the configuration of constraint programming or mathematical optimization solvers (see, e.g., [4]), the hyperparameter tuning of ML pipelines, the administration of ad-hoc medical treatments, and many others; for a more detailed treatment of the subject, the interested reader is referred, e.g., to [5,2] and the references therein.

In this article, we supply a comprehensive framework for describing any approach to the ACP: we identify the core building components for designing an ACP solution strategy, and discuss their possible use patterns and implementation.

References:
[1] Gupta, R., Roughgarden, T.: A PAC approach to application-specific algorithm selection. In: Proceedings of the 2016 ACM Conference on Innovations in Theoretical Computer Science. pp. 123––134. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA (2016)
[2] Kerschke, P., Hoos, H.H., Neumann, F., Trautmann, H.: Automated Algorithm Selection: Survey and Perspectives. Evolutionary Computation 27 (1), 3–45 (2019)
[3] Rice, J.R.: The algorithm selection problem. Advances in Computers 15 , 65–118 (1976)
[4] Liu, J., , Ploskas, N., Sahinidis, N.V.: Tuning baron using derivative-free optimization algorithms. Journal of Global Optimization 74 (4), 611––637 (2019)
[5] Eggensperger, K., Lindauer, M., Hutter, F.: Pitfalls and best practices in algorithm configuration. Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 64 (1), 861––893 (2019)
